"Bitcoin XT contains an unmentioned addition which periodically downloads lists of Tor IP addresses for blacklisting."
It's not exactly unmentioned. It is on their features list and described in detail on their Github page.
Mentioned or unmentioned, it fundamentally changes what XT is argued to be about. It's hard not to be suspicious of the motivations involved, and what actors may be behind the scenes.

XT was never supposed to be just about big blocks, it was a place for experimental features that might later be integrated in to bitcoin core.

However, if you want to just support big blocks with out all the other experimental features you can go here: https://github.com/bitcoinxt/bitcoinxt/tree/only-bigblocks

It is reason to be curious about their motivations, but I don't find it as tempting to be suspicious. They have said it was part of an anti-DDOS measure that would be replaced by something more sophisticated in the future. While you might disagree with their means, I have no reason to doubt their sincerity.
I'm pretty cool with the block size increase, but this is just pure bullshit.
If this is true then BitcoinXT has failed before it even gets off the ground.

It's not unmentioned and it's not something sinister. It's designed to prevent your node from getting flooded with bogus connection requests. Dos attacks generally come from Tor users so all it's doing is when your connection slots get used up any Tor connections get a lower priority to connect to your node. It's a good feature!

It's nothing different than the current Bitcoin Core that also blacklist's ip addresses that misbehave.

Blacklisting is a very sinister term for what is happening. It does not disallow connections from tor nodes. People that are trying to push this are wrong. It's a priority list. It puts tor nodes at the bottom so of a DoS connection attack starts, it will drop tor nodes first. This should never happen under normal operation.

Upon first hearing about it, I was quite concerned about the DoS patch in Bitcoin XT. I had actually begun writing a big post to Mike addressing the issue. But I found this post and it has dramatically calmed me down about the patch:

http://imgur.com/gallery/LX11bIT/new

The key part is highlighted in yellow, but I suggest reading the entire thing because it explains why and how it came to be. It makes a lot more sense.

A node has a maximum number of 125 incoming connections. These would only typically be all full if a DoS attack was occuring. The DoS patch ONLY becomes active when all 125 incoming connections are full. Otherwise it does nothing. So in ordinary circumstances when no attack is occuring, the patch doesn't even run at all.

You can disable this feature if you really want to, by using the flag: -disableipprio

TL/DR: There's a lot of FUD being spread to try to discredit Bitcoin XT. Do your research, starting with the above link

From the BXT website: "Anti-DoS attack improvements, by Mike Hearn. It's currently possible to jam a Bitcoin node by connecting to it repeatedly via different IP addresses, as there is a fixed limit on how many connections a node will accept. Once full, no other peers or wallets can connect to it any more and serving capacity for new nodes and P2P wallets is reduced. If the attack is repeated against every node, the entire network could become jammed.

This patch set introduces code that runs when a node is full and otherwise could not accept new connections. It labels and prioritises connections according to lists of IP ranges: if a high priority IP address connects and the node is full, it will disconnect a lower priority connection to make room. Currently Tor exits are labelled as being lower priority than regular IP addresses, as jamming attacks via Tor have been observed, and most users/merchants don't use it. In normal operation this new code will never run. If someone performs a DoS attack via Tor, then legitimate Tor users will get the existing behaviour of being unable to connect, but mobile and home users will still be able to use the network without disruption."

So. This code only comes into effect once a node's connection list is full, which most likely means it's being DoSed and basically all it does is set tor exit node IPs (which are periodically downloaded because they change) to low priority, since that's where the DoS attacks are currently coming from, so that regular IPs are given preference such that regular users and cell phone wallets are not disconnected. The downside of this code is that in the event that this code is run, a legitimate user on tor could be disconnected in favor of a user with a regular IP. Hearn has stated that this possibility is minuscule as not many people use tor with bitcoin and if you want anonymity with bitcoin, a vpn still works just fine and is the preferred method of anonymity for most users anyway...

In the first paragraph from the linux foundation it says it's "unmentioned" and then later in the same paragraph it says it's "claimed anti-DoS measures". How can it be unmentioned but also claimed ant-DoS measures? If they claim that it's anti-DoS measures THAT'S FUCKING MENTIONING IT. This article is alarmist drivel IMO.

unmentioned addition

Mike Hearn talks about the function on the website. It's an Anti-Dos attack feature.

11/10 FUD rating.

This code prioritizes the IP addresses of nodes known to behave correctly according to Mike Hearn, and drops deprioritized nodes when the machine runs out of resources. This could eventually lead XT nodes to only connect to "white-listed" peers, essentially forcing users to use specific access points to relay transactions to the network. In fact XT contains a Python script which generates a C struct of deprioritized IP's specifically mapped from TOR exits. As of the publication of shitco.in's article the XT project has a list of over 1000 IP's which have been added to this blacklist.

One can easily see how this mechanism could serve a regime in regulating the use of Bitcoin at the protocol level, a step beyond even what Coinbase has done.

Source: Qntra.
